## Set Theory Fundamentals

This note collects the basic vocabulary and operations of naïve
[[set-theory|set theory]] that are used throughout analysis and measure theory.
De Morgan's laws, which relate unions, intersections and complements, are
included under *Algebra of Sets* below.

## Sets and Subsets

:::{.definition data-title="Set, Subset, Power Set"}

A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, called its **elements**. We write
$x\in A$ if $x$ is an element of $A$. The **empty set** $\emptyset$ has no
elements. A set $A$ is a **subset** of $B$, written $A\subseteq B$, if
$x\in A\implies x\in B$. Two sets are **equal** if and only if
$A\subseteq B$ and $B\subseteq A$. The **power set** of $X$ is the collection
of all subsets of $X$,
$$
2^X:=\{A: A\subseteq X\}.
$$

:::

> *Note:* If $X$ is finite with $n$ elements then $\lvert 2^X\rvert=2^n$, which
motivates the notation $2^X$.

Throughout, we fix an ambient **universe** set $X$ and consider subsets of $X$.

## Set Operations

:::{.definition data-title="Set Operations"}

For $A,B\subseteq X$ we define the

- **union** $A\cup B:=\{x: x\in A \text{ or } x\in B\}$;
- **intersection** $A\cap B:=\{x: x\in A \text{ and } x\in B\}$;
- **complement** $A^c:=\{x\in X: x\notin A\}$;
- **difference** $A\setminus B:=\{x: x\in A \text{ and } x\notin B\}=A\cap B^c$;
- **symmetric difference** $A\triangle B:=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)$.

:::

## Indexed Families

:::{.definition data-title="Arbitrary Unions and Intersections"}

Let $\{A_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I}$ be a family of subsets of $X$ indexed by a set
$I$. Then
$$
\bigcup_{\alpha\in I}A_\alpha:=\{x: x\in A_\alpha \text{ for some }\alpha\in I\},
\qquad
\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}A_\alpha:=\{x: x\in A_\alpha \text{ for all }\alpha\in I\}.
$$

:::

When $I=\mathbb{N}$ we have a **countable** union or intersection, which is the
form that appears in the definition of a $\sigma$-algebra.

## Algebra of Sets

:::{.theorem data-title="Algebra of Sets"}

For $A,B,C\subseteq X$:

1. **Commutativity:** $A\cup B=B\cup A$ and $A\cap B=B\cap A$.
2. **Associativity:** $(A\cup B)\cup C=A\cup(B\cup C)$ and
   $(A\cap B)\cap C=A\cap(B\cap C)$.
3. **Distributivity:**
   $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$ and
   $A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)$.
4. **Complements:** $(A^c)^c=A$, $A\cup A^c=X$, $A\cap A^c=\emptyset$.
5. **De Morgan:** $\left(\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\right)^c=\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha^c$
   and $\left(\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha\right)^c=\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha^c$.

:::

:::{.proof}
Each identity is proved by double inclusion: take an arbitrary $x$ in the
left-hand side and show it lies in the right-hand side, then vice versa. For
example, for the first distributive law,
$$
x\in A\cap(B\cup C)\iff x\in A \text{ and } (x\in B \text{ or } x\in C)
\iff (x\in A\cap B) \text{ or } (x\in A\cap C).
$$
:::

## Disjoint Unions and Partitions

:::{.definition data-title="Disjoint Family and Partition"}

Sets $A,B$ are **disjoint** if $A\cap B=\emptyset$. A family
$\{A_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I}$ is **pairwise disjoint** if $A_\alpha\cap A_\beta=\emptyset$
for all $\alpha\neq\beta$. We write $A\sqcup B$ or $\bigsqcup_\alpha A_\alpha$ for
a union that is known to be disjoint. A **partition** of $X$ is a pairwise
disjoint family of nonempty sets whose union is $X$.

:::

Any union can be made disjoint: given $\{A_n\}_{n\geq1}$, set
$B_1=A_1$ and $B_n=A_n\setminus\bigcup_{k<n}A_k$. Then the $B_n$ are pairwise
disjoint and $\bigcup_nB_n=\bigcup_nA_n$. This trick is used constantly to
reduce statements about measures of countable unions to countable additivity.

## Cartesian Products

:::{.definition data-title="Cartesian Product"}

The **Cartesian product** of sets $A$ and $B$ is the set of ordered pairs
$$
A\times B:=\{(a,b): a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
$$
More generally, for an indexed family, $\prod_{\alpha\in I}A_\alpha$ is the set
of functions $x$ on $I$ with $x(\alpha)\in A_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$. We write
$A^n=A\times\cdots\times A$.

:::

## Monotone Sequences of Sets

:::{.definition data-title="Monotone Sequence of Sets"}

A sequence $\{A_n\}_{n\geq1}$ is **increasing** if $A_n\subseteq A_{n+1}$ for all
$n$, in which case we write $A_n\uparrow A$ with $A=\bigcup_nA_n$. It is
**decreasing** if $A_{n+1}\subseteq A_n$ for all $n$, in which case we write
$A_n\downarrow A$ with $A=\bigcap_nA_n$.

:::

Monotone sequences are the sets analogue of monotone real sequences, and they
are the setting for continuity from below and above of measures.
